title: No. 36 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: We have seen that the previous paper's analysis leads to this conclusion: from the natural operation of the different interests and views of the various classes of the community, whether representation is more or less numerous, it will consist almost entirely of landowners, merchants, and members of the learned professions, who will truly represent all those different interests and views. If someone objects that we have seen other types of men in local legislatures, I admit there are exceptions to the rule, but not enough to influence the general character of the government. Strong minds in every walk of life will rise above the disadvantages of their situation and command the respect due to their merit, not only from their own class but from society in general. The door should be equally open to all. I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we will see such vigorous plants flourishing in federal as well as state legislation. But occasional examples of this sort will not weaken the reasoning based on the general course of things.

The subject could be viewed in many other ways that all lead to the same result. In particular, what greater similarity or shared interest is there between the carpenter and blacksmith, or the linen weaver and stocking maker, than between the merchant and any of them? It is well known that there are often as great rivalries between different branches of mechanical or manufacturing arts as between any departments of labor. Unless the representative body were far more numerous than is consistent with orderly or wise deliberation, what seems to be the spirit of this objection could never be realized in practice. But I will not dwell longer on a matter that has so far worn too loose a garment to allow accurate inspection of its real shape or tendency.

There is another, more precise objection that demands our attention. It has been claimed that the national legislature could never exercise an internal taxing power effectively, both from a lack of local knowledge and from interference between Union and state revenue laws. The supposition of inadequate knowledge appears entirely unfounded. If a question arises in a state legislature about one of its counties that requires local detail, how is that knowledge obtained? No doubt from the members representing that county. Can't similar knowledge be obtained in the national legislature from each state's representatives? And isn't it likely that the men sent there will have the necessary intelligence to communicate that information? Is local knowledge for taxation purposes a minute topographical familiarity with every mountain, river, stream, highway, and byway in each state? Or is it a general knowledge of the state's situation and resources, of its agriculture, commerce, manufactures, of the nature of its products and consumption, and of its different kinds of wealth, property, and industry?

Even under the most popular forms of government, nations usually entrust the administration of their finances to single individuals or to boards of a few people. These prepare the plans of taxation, which are then passed into law by the sovereign or legislature.

Inquisitive and enlightened statesmen are everywhere considered best qualified to make a judicious selection of revenue sources. This shows clearly, as far as the general sense of mankind has weight, what kind of local knowledge is needed for taxation purposes.

Internal taxes can be divided into direct and indirect kinds. Though both face objection, the reasoning seems confined to the former. As for the latter, by which we mean duties and excises on consumption, it is hard to see what difficulties are feared. The relevant knowledge will either be suggested by the article itself or easily obtained from any well-informed person, especially from the mercantile class. The differences between the article's situation in different states must be few, simple, and easy to grasp. The main thing to attend to would be avoiding articles already taxed by particular states. There would be no difficulty in determining each state's revenue system, since this can always be known from each state's laws and from its representatives.

The objection seems more substantial when applied to real property like houses and land, but even here it doesn't survive close examination. Land taxes are usually laid in one of two ways: either by actual valuations, permanent or periodic, or by occasional assessments at the discretion of officers whose duty it is to make them. In either case, the execution of the work, which alone requires local knowledge, must be assigned to discreet persons acting as commissioners or assessors, elected by the people or appointed by the government. All the law can do is name the persons or prescribe how they will be elected or appointed, fix their numbers and qualifications, and outline their general powers and duties. What is there in all this that the national legislature cannot do as well as a state legislature? Either can only address general principles. Local details, as already noted, must be left to those who execute the plan.

But there is a simple way to view this matter that should be entirely satisfactory. The national legislature can use the system of each state within that state. The method of laying and collecting these taxes in each state can be adopted and used in all its parts by the federal government.

Remember that the proportion of these taxes is not left to the national legislature's discretion. It is determined by the number of people in each state, as described in the second section of the first article. An actual census must furnish the rule, which effectively shuts the door to partiality or oppression. The abuse of this taxing power has been guarded against with careful precaution. In addition to what I just mentioned, there is a provision that "all duties, imposts, and excises shall be UNIFORM throughout the United States."

Various speakers and writers favoring the Constitution have rightly noted that if the Union's exercise of internal taxation should prove inconvenient in practice, the federal government may simply refrain from using it and rely on requisitions instead. To this it has been triumphantly asked: Why not omit that ambiguous power from the start and rely on the latter? Two solid answers can be given. First, exercising the power, if convenient, would be preferable because it would be more effective. It is impossible to prove in theory, rather than by experiment, that it cannot be exercised advantageously. The contrary seems most probable. Second, the existence of such a power in the Constitution will strongly encourage compliance with requisitions. When states know the Union can act without their cooperation, they will be powerfully motivated to do their part.

As for interference between the revenue laws of the Union and its members, we have already seen there can be no clash or conflict of authority. The laws cannot, therefore, in a legal sense, interfere with each other. It is far from impossible to avoid interference even in the policy of their different systems. An effective method will be for each side to mutually abstain from objects the other has first used. Since neither can control the other, each will have an obvious interest in this reciprocal restraint. Where there is an immediate common interest, we may safely count on its operation. When the particular debts of the states are eliminated and their expenses limited to their natural compass, the possibility of interference will almost vanish. A small land tax will serve the states' purposes and be their simplest and most fitting resource.

Many ghosts have been raised from this internal taxing power to alarm the people: double sets of revenue officers, a doubling of burdens through double taxation, and the frightful forms of odious and oppressive poll taxes have been paraded with all the clever sleight-of-hand of political illusion.

On the first point, there are two cases where there can be no room for double sets of officers. One is where the right to impose the tax is exclusively vested in the Union, as with import duties. The other is where the object has not fallen under any state regulation, which may apply to many objects. In other cases, the United States will probably either wholly avoid objects already used for local purposes, or use state officers and regulations to collect the additional levy. This will best serve the goals of revenue, since it saves collection expenses and best avoids any cause for resentment in state governments and the people. In any event, here is a workable way to avoid this inconvenience. Nothing more can be required than to show that the predicted evils don't necessarily follow from the plan.

As to any argument from a supposed scheme of influence, it is enough to say it should not be presumed. But the supposition can be answered more precisely. If such a spirit infested the councils of the Union, the surest way to its goal would be to employ state officers as much as possible and bind them to the Union by accumulating their salaries. This would turn state influence into channels serving the national government, rather than making federal influence flow in an opposite, hostile current. But all such suppositions are invidious and should be banished from consideration of this great question. They serve no purpose but to cast a mist over the truth.

As to the suggestion of double taxation, the answer is plain. The needs of the Union must be met one way or another. If by federal authority, then not by state authority. The total taxes paid by the community will be the same in either case. With the advantage that, if provision is made by the Union, the major resource of commercial duties (the most convenient branch of revenue) can be developed much more fully under federal than under state regulation. This will of course make resorting to less convenient methods less necessary. With this further advantage: as far as there may be real difficulty in exercising internal taxing power, it will impose greater care in choosing and arranging the means. It must naturally make it a fixed point of national policy to go as far as practicable in making the luxury of the rich a tribute to the public treasury, in order to reduce the need for taxes that might cause dissatisfaction in the poorer and most numerous classes. Happy it is when the government's interest in preserving its own power coincides with a proper distribution of public burdens, and tends to guard the least wealthy from oppression!

As to poll taxes, I confess without scruple my disapproval of them. Though they have prevailed from an early period in those states which have always been most tenacious of their rights, I would lament to see them introduced under the national government. But does it follow because there is power to lay them that they will actually be laid? Every state in the Union has power to impose taxes of this kind, yet in several of them they are unknown in practice. Are state governments to be branded as tyrannies because they possess this power? If not, with what propriety can the same power justify such a charge against the national government, or be urged as an obstacle to its adoption? As little as I favor this kind of tax, I am thoroughly convinced that the power to resort to it should exist in the federal government. Nations have certain emergencies in which expedients that would normally be avoided become essential to the public welfare. The government, in case of such emergencies, should always have the option of using them. The real scarcity of objects in this country that can be considered productive sources of revenue is a reason peculiar to itself for not abridging the discretion of the national councils on this point. There may exist certain critical and stormy situations in which a poll tax may become an invaluable resource. Since I know nothing to exempt this part of the world from the common calamities that have befallen others, I confess my aversion to every project that would disarm the government of a single weapon which, in any possible contingency, might be usefully employed for general defense and security.

(I have now examined the powers proposed to be vested in the United States that have an immediate relation to the energy of the government, and have tried to answer the principal objections raised against them. I have passed over those minor authorities which are either too inconsiderable to have provoked the hostility of the Constitution's opponents, or of too obvious propriety to admit of controversy. The mass of judicial power might have warranted investigation under this head, except that its organization and extent may be more advantageously considered together. This has led me to refer it to the next branch of our inquiry.)

(I have now examined those powers proposed to be conferred on the federal government which relate especially to its energy and to its effectiveness for accomplishing the great primary objects of union. There are others which, though omitted here, will be addressed under the next head of our inquiry to render the picture complete. I flatter myself that the progress already made will satisfy the candid and judicious part of the community that some of the objections most strenuously urged against the Constitution, and most formidable at first appearance, are not only without substance, but if they had operated in forming the plan, would have made it incapable of achieving the great ends of public happiness and national prosperity. I equally flatter myself that further critical investigation of the system will recommend it still more to every sincere and disinterested advocate of good government, and will leave no doubt with such men of the propriety and expediency of adopting it. Happy will it be for ourselves, and more honorable for human nature, if we have wisdom and virtue enough to set so glorious an example to mankind!)
1. The New England States.
